comment_text: The article outlines and explains a few very valid points, but I have a little tension with some. It starts off with, “We tell young artists never to pay for the privilege of being considered.” It explains when this general idea is and is not applied, and I mostly agree, but not fully. Being an artist requires financial investment in visibility. This is a fact. Media outlets are dying and arts reporting is mostly cut first. Small and medium size galleries are struggling unless they are supported by the very top collectors and investors, and competition for survival is brutal. Artists are told never to pay for the “privilege” of being considered. The wrong word is “privilege,” because that’s not what survival is about. Transparency is crucial, you should know what you are paying for, and who you work with should be reputable. But the association of privilege with participation is ignoring the realities of the art market that’s outside of its most elite nook. But bad players should always be held accountable, that much is absolutely true.

The model can be criticized for opacity, weak selection standards, or the inflation of “visibility” as a promise. But when the fee remains operationally modest, payment alone does not constitute exclusion.

post_text: Something to consider before engaging a recruiting firm for your next hire… Not all recruiting firms operate the same way. Here’s what often separates a smaller, local firm from a large national agency: 1) Experience With a smaller firm, you’re typically working directly with a recruiter who has 15–20+ years of experience — not a junior recruiter measured solely on daily call quotas. 2) Performance metrics vs. activity metrics. Large firms often track: – Calls made – Resumes sent – Submittals per week Smaller firms focus on: – Submission-to-interview ratios – Interview-to-offer ratios – 6–12 month retention of placements It’s not about volume. It’s about accuracy. 3) Local market intelligence. Compensation trends. Bonus timing. Who’s open to hybrid. What it actually takes to close the right candidate. If you value quality, accountability, and a true hiring partner — not just resume flow — a smaller local firm may be your strongest advantage.

Large firms often track: – Calls made – Resumes sent – Submittals per week Smaller firms focus on: – Submission-to-interview ratios – Interview-to-offer ratios – 6–12 month retention of placements It’s not about volume. It’s about accuracy. 3) Local market intelligence. Compensation trends. Bonus timing. Who’s open to hybrid. What it actually takes to close the right candidate. If you value quality, accountability, and a true hiring partner — not just resume flow — a smaller local firm may be your strongest advantage.

post_text: Most companies automatically choose a big recruitment agency over a solo recruiter. ✅ More consultants ✅ Bigger brand ✅ Fancy office ✅ Coffee machines with more buttons than a keyboard But here’s what no one likes saying out loud… A solo recruiter will often work harder on your role than an entire agency team. Something to be layered on top of years of people, processes, systems, and tech debt. But what if AI isn’t the destination? What if it’s the starting point? The Next Google Won’t Look Like the Last One Google once started with two people in a garage. Today, the same thing is happening again—quietly. There are small, scrappy companies being built right now where: AI is first, not last Processes are designed around automation Speed is native, not forced Cost structures are lean by default They don’t need to unwind legacy workflows. They don’t need to retrain thousands of people. They don’t need multi-year transformation programs. They just… build. Incumbents vs AI-Native Startups Large firms have scale, brand, relationships, and capital. But they also have complexity. AI-native startups have none of that—and that’s the advantage. They can move faster. They can experiment cheaper. They can redesign recruiting from first principles instead of retrofitting it. In staffing and recruiting, that speed matters. Time-to-fill, cost-to-hire, candidate experience—AI-first players can rethink all of it from day one. The Question Leaders Should Be Asking This isn’t about buying more tools or spending more money. It’s about mindset. How do we think more like a startup inside a scaled business? Where can we adopt instead of build? Where is complexity self-inflicted? What would we design differently if we were starting today? Because the biggest risk isn’t that big firms won’t adopt AI. It’s that smaller, AI-native players will never need to catch up. Final Thought Disruption rarely announces itself. It shows up lean, fast, and underestimated. The winners won’t be the companies with the most AI slides. They’ll be the ones willing to unlearn first. Curious what others think: Can large staffing firms truly think like startups—or is the next wave already being built in garages again? 👇 Let’s debate.

post_text: This niche fire protection engineer got lowballed. He was promised $152K during the interview process. Then leadership stepped in: “We’ll offer $134K.” Recently, I was working with a large organisation on finding their next fire protection lead. This is a super niche role, and finding a fire protection engineer of this calibre is no small task. The talent pool is tight. The experience required is specific. And the right people aren’t actively applying for jobs. After months of searching, we finally found the guy. Perfect technical background. Strong leadership credibility. Available at the right time. The fire protection department manager met him, loved him, and they aligned on $152K. Handshake agreement. Everyone was on the same page. Then senior leadership reviewed the package. “We’re not comfortable at $152K. Let’s formalise at $134K.” We pushed back. Hard. But the response was: “We can’t disrupt our internal salary bandings for one hire.” When we went back to the candidate, his reaction was simple: “We already agreed terms. Why are we renegotiating?” I had to explain that the offer had been overridden internally. He walked. And I couldn’t blame him. This was a six-month search for an incredibly hard-to-fill fire protection position. In their justification, they benchmarked the role against other engineering disciplines, ignoring the fact that fire protection sits in its own market, with its own supply-and-demand pressures. On paper, it probably looked like they were saving $18K. In reality, they lost half a year of work and credibility with a well-connected professional in a tight-knit industry. When you’re hiring in fire protection, market rate isn’t a suggestion. It’s the cost of entry. Ignore it at your own cost.

post_text: One of the biggest pain points in the recruiting community? Recruiters can't get hired themselves. And the reasons? Wildly contradictory. Same recruiter. Same profile. Same experience. Company A → You're overqualified. Company B → You're underqualified. Company C → You haven't worked in our market. Company D → You've only done tech hiring. Company E → You've only done non-tech hiring. Company F → You don't have campus hiring experience. Company G → You haven't done GTM hiring before. Company H → You've never hired for leadership roles. Company I → You don't have volume hiring experience. Company J → You've only done niche hiring. And the list goes on… I'm sorry — how does this make sense? 🤔 The same person is too much for one and not enough for another? Think about what a recruiter actually does. Sourced. Screened. Convinced. Closed. For roles THEY have never personally done themselves. They figured out tech hiring without being a techie. They figured out niche markets without being a subject expert. They walked into the unknown and delivered. That IS the skill. So when an experienced recruiter applies to a new market why is that suddenly too big an ask? The irony is hard to ignore. We trust recruiters to judge talent every single day. But when THEY are the candidate, nothing is ever quite right. post_text: “Estate agency is easy money” I hear it all the time. What people see: • A board goes up • A property goes online • It sells or lets • Commission gets paid What they don’t see: • Deals collapsing weeks before completion • Chains breaking • Late night negotiations • Viewings after hours • Difficult conversations about price • Managing emotions on both sides This job isn’t about opening doors. No salary for “almost sold.” No commission for “nearly exchanged.” Good agents aren’t money hungry. They’re value driven. Because reputation travels fast in this industry, especially when you’re independent. #estateagentmyths #ukproperty #salesandlettings #realestate #propertyinsights

post_text: “We can’t find skilled tradespeople.” Translation: “We posted the job, waited three weeks, offered 2019 wages… and now we’re confused.” Let’s be honest for a second. The labor market didn’t disappear. It evolved. Right now: • Welders know exactly what the shop down the street is paying. • Maintenance techs compare overtime structures like fantasy football stats. • Engineers won’t wait 4 weeks for a second interview. • The best foremen are recruited before their boots hit the parking lot. And yet some companies are still hiring like it’s 2008. My favorite is: “Must have 10 years of experience, be proficient in everything, willing to work weekends… budget is tight though.” That’s not a job description. post_text: Everyone says that LinkedIn is the best platform for remote roles but I 100% disagree 👀 Don't get me wrong—LinkedIn is great. The hidden remote job market: VC-backed startups While everyone's refreshing LinkedIn Jobs and competing with 500+ applicants, there's a goldmine of opportunities hiding in plain sight. Read their funding announcement to understand their growth plans. Reference their recent funding round and explain how you can help them scale. You'll stand out because you did your homework. Why this approach wins: ✅ Zero competition (no job post = no applicants) ✅ Shows initiative and strategic thinking ✅ Startups move fast—they'll create roles for the right fit ✅ Remote-first is standard in VC-backed tech companies Pro tip: Set up Google Alerts for "[Your industry] Series A/B/C funding" and be the first to reach out. The best remote roles? They're never posted on LinkedIn. comment_text: There’s a subtle economic nuance embedded in the “who is the product” framing. In the traditional recruiting model, the candidate is still the product — presented, evaluated, and ultimately “purchased” by the employer. The *company* simply funds the search. Reverse recruiting doesn’t eliminate that dynamic. It shifts **who pays for representation,** not who functions as the asset being matched. Which makes this trend read much more like a talent-agent model — similar to what we see in professional sports. ✅ Recruiters resemble scouts working for **the team** (company). 🔺 Reverse recruiters resemble **agents** working for **the player** (candidate). That distinction matters because it changes expectations. ◀️ Especially at the leadership level, the meaningful success metric isn’t interview volume. It’s offer conversion.** Interviews can be generated. Offers remain market-driven decisions. I cover the "talent agent" vs "talent scout" model in a Forbes Coaches Council article, Feb 2024. https://www.forbes.com/councils/forbescoachescouncil/2024/02/21/will-an-executive-recruiter-find-a-job-for-me-3-recruitment-models-and-how-to-leverage-relationships-with-recruiters/

comment_text: AI has flooded the system on both ends: Job seekers widely use tools like ChatGPT to generate resumes, cover letters, and even interview prep (often 60-90% of applicants in surveys). This creates a massive volume of applications…many generic or “AI-optimized” for keyword matching in applicant tracking systems (ATS). Recruiters and companies respond by tightening AI filters, adding more screening layers, or ghosting more aggressively to cope with the noise. The result is a vicious cycle: more applications…worse signal-to-noise...longer searches, higher rejection rates, and widespread frustration. Studies and articles describe this as an “arms race” or “doom loop” that makes hiring miserable and less human.

post_text: The number of Recruiters who cannot recruit beyond posting a job is honestly alarming. Companies are paying agency fees up to 30 percent of a Candidate’s annual salary and in many cases the hiring manager could have found that same person on LinkedIn in about ten minutes. Posting and praying is not recruiting. Real recruiting is identifying a market, mapping competitors, engaging passive Candidates, qualifying motivations, and managing both sides of the process from first conversation to acceptance. It is business development, relationship building, and influence. Not an Indeed notification. Large agency training used to create true Recruiters. People who knew how to open doors, run a search, and create value for a client. Somewhere along the way the model shifted to volume activity and software alerts. If your entire desk stops working when you do not have a job order to post, you do not have a recruiting business. You have a posting habit. Clients pay fees for access, insight, and control of the hiring process. When you actually recruit, you earn it and everyone wins. Experienced Recruiters who still believe in building a real desk know exactly what I am talking about.

comment_text: This resonates. 11+ years in agency recruiting and business development taught me that real recruiting was never “post and pray.” It was market mapping, competitor analysis, passive outreach, and relationship building long before a job order ever hit the desk. I do think COVID accelerated a major shift. Many experienced headhunters exited the industry, teams downsized, and volume became the priority over strategy. At the same time, many organizations became heavily dependent on AI tools, resume scanning, automated rejections, workflow automation, which increased efficiency but reduced human interaction. AI should enhance recruiting, not replace discernment. When algorithms filter before a recruiter even reviews a profile, you risk missing high-potential talent. And when recruiters are buried in back-to-back meetings and administrative tasks, they don’t have the time to truly headhunt. That’s not an individual failure it’s often structural.The best recruiters still build pipelines before they’re needed. They still strategically source. They take time to study each role deeply and create intentional hiring plans. They continuously build strong relationships with candidates and clients not just when there’s an opening, but always.

post_text: They hired their first recruiter from Google. Three months into Series A, hiring had stalled. She’d hired hundreds of engineers before. But this was a different game. At Google, engineers apply. Thousands of them. Your job is to filter. At a 30-person startup nobody has heard of, nobody is applying. Your job is to create demand. Two different muscles. Neither better. Just different. At Series A, you don’t need pedigree. You need someone who can build pull from zero. Someone comfortable reaching out cold. Someone who can make candidates reconsider their plans. That rarely shows up on a CV. And it’s usually the difference between stalled hiring and real momentum.
comment_text: So true. Startup hiring is far more human than transactional. It’s not about screening from a pile of resumes, it’s about sparking belief in something that doesn’t yet have a brand, a name, or a crowd behind it. The real skill is convincing great talent to take a leap of faith.

comment_text: Interesting take — but I slightly disagree. Having worked in both environments, I don’t think this is purely a big company vs startup muscle problem. At companies like Google, yes, there’s massive inbound and filtering becomes a core skill. But the best recruiters there don’t just filter — they still build relationships, convince passive talent, and shape decisions. Similarly in early-stage startups, while creating demand is critical, the real differentiator isn’t where someone comes from. It’s obsession with the craft. The recruiters who succeed — whether at a 30-person Series A startup or a global tech company — are the ones who treat recruiting like a problem to solve every day. They learn the market, understand talent psychology, and keep refining how they engage candidates. Skills can travel. Pedigree doesn’t decide outcomes. Obsession does.

Yet, this is exactly what happens in IT hiring every day. Hiring managers and teams get so hyper-focused on whether a candidate has used one specific, niche tool or framework that they completely miss the bigger picture. Technology changes constantly. The specific "car" your team is driving today probably won't be the one you're driving in three years. If someone is a great driver who understands the mechanics of the road and knows how to read the manual, they can drive your tech stack. Let's stop hiring for matching acronyms on a resume and start hiring for adaptability, fundamentals, and problem-solving mileage.

post_text: Most companies automatically choose a big recruitment agency over a solo recruiter. ✅ More consultants ✅ Bigger brand ✅ Fancy office ✅ Coffee machines with more buttons than a keyboard But here’s what no one likes saying out loud… A solo recruiter will often work harder on your role than an entire agency team. Why? Because when a big firm takes your role, the recruiter has to work twice as fast and juggle dozens of clients just to cover the 80% fee they lose to their employer. They might say they’re your trusted recruitment partner… But they’re saying the same thing to 30+ other clients. When a solo recruiter takes your role… 😀 Your role pays our bills 😀 Your role keeps our business open 😀 Your role keeps our dream alive So ask yourself this: Who is going to value your role more? And while we’re here, let’s kill another myth. There is no secret candidate database. Every recruiter is using the same tools: 🔎 LinkedIn 🔎 Job boards 🔎 Referrals 🔎 Internal databases The difference isn’t access. It’s hunger. When companies say they have “a bajillion candidates on their database”, it means nothing if they’re outdated, irrelevant, or in the wrong sector. Yet companies still default to the biggest agency in the room because it feels safer. Next time you need recruitment support, ask a different question. Not “How big is your database?” Ask “How quickly do you get people hired?” As a solo recruiter, my average time to offer is under 20 days. It doesn’t matter if my database has 10 candidates or 10 million. What matters is getting the right one. We all say we should support independent businesses. But apparently that rule doesn’t always apply to recruiters. Just my view 😀 #Recruitment #Hiring #SoloRecruiter #AgencyLife #AndrewsRecruitmentGroup
comment_text: The difference is more than hunger. Successful recruiters follow a science. A structured process that allows them to perform in any organisation. Like any business, people are critical to success, but it’s the efficiency of the systems and processes behind them that enable consistent results. A “hungry” individual without a process simply runs around like a headless chicken.

comment_text: That's a great question. My TA experience is mainly in STEM start-up and SME employers, and I'd work with a small number of strategic partners where I had limited capacity or for specialist functions. I find four measures to be helpful in looking at new and existing suppliers: 1: Ratio of CVs sent to final interview. I find this highlights accuracy of provision, given CVs to 1st interview is often as much about how compelling the representation is. 2: 1st year performance of the employee vs expectation for the vacancy. It's longer term, but valuable, particularly for key hires 3: Quality of their job adverts or, if they don't advertise publicly, evidence of their written outreach. Great way to see how they advocate the business - is it copy+paste and a "my favourite client" or does it show your context & values with what good really looks like in qualified candidates? 4: What do candidates think of the agencies? Not do they like them, but how transparent and responsive are they, how did they support and guide them? Perhaps my TA network can share ideas - Simon Amesbury, Julie Wilcock, Charlotte Steggall, Kasha I.

post_text: This niche fire protection engineer got lowballed. He was promised $152K during the interview process. Then leadership stepped in: “We’ll offer $134K.” Recently, I was working with a large organisation on finding their next fire protection lead. This is a super niche role, and finding a fire protection engineer of this calibre is no small task. The talent pool is tight. The experience required is specific. And the right people aren’t actively applying for jobs. After months of searching, we finally found the guy. Perfect technical background. Strong leadership credibility. Available at the right time. The fire protection department manager met him, loved him, and they aligned on $152K. Handshake agreement. Everyone was on the same page. Then senior leadership reviewed the package. “We’re not comfortable at $152K. Let’s formalise at $134K.” We pushed back. Hard. But the response was: “We can’t disrupt our internal salary bandings for one hire.” When we went back to the candidate, his reaction was simple: “We already agreed terms. Why are we renegotiating?” I had to explain that the offer had been overridden internally. He walked. And I couldn’t blame him. This was a six-month search for an incredibly hard-to-fill fire protection position. In their justification, they benchmarked the role against other engineering disciplines, ignoring the fact that fire protection sits in its own market, with its own supply-and-demand pressures. On paper, it probably looked like they were saving $18K. In reality, they lost half a year of work and credibility with a well-connected professional in a tight-knit industry. When you’re hiring in fire protection, market rate isn’t a suggestion. It’s the cost of entry. Ignore it at your own cost.

post_text: “Estate agency is easy money” I hear it all the time. What people see: • A board goes up • A property goes online • It sells or lets • Commission gets paid What they don’t see: • Deals collapsing weeks before completion • Chains breaking • Late night negotiations • Viewings after hours • Difficult conversations about price • Managing emotions on both sides This job isn’t about opening doors. It’s managing risk, expectations, and problems while protecting clients from expensive mistakes. And here’s the truth most don’t realise: We only get paid if it works. No salary for “almost sold.” No commission for “nearly exchanged.” Good agents aren’t money hungry. They’re value driven. Because reputation travels fast in this industry, especially when you’re independent. #estateagentmyths #ukproperty #salesandlettings #realestate #propertyinsights

post_text: Everyone says that LinkedIn is the best platform for remote roles but I 100% disagree 👀 Don't get me wrong—LinkedIn is great. But if you're only applying to jobs here, you're missing the biggest opportunity. The hidden remote job market: VC-backed startups While everyone's refreshing LinkedIn Jobs and competing with 500+ applicants, there's a goldmine of opportunities hiding in plain sight. Here's what smart job seekers do: 1️⃣ Follow the money Head to Crunchbase or TechCrunch's funding roundups. Filter for companies that raised funding in the last 90 days. These startups just got capital to scale their teams—they NEED to hire, fast. 2️⃣ Get there before the job post Check their careers page and LinkedIn company profile. Read their funding announcement to understand their growth plans. Most haven't even written the job descriptions yet. 3️⃣ Reach out directly Message their Head of [Your Department] or hiring managers. Reference their recent funding round and explain how you can help them scale. You'll stand out because you did your homework. Why this approach wins: ✅ Zero competition (no job post = no applicants) ✅ Shows initiative and strategic thinking ✅ Startups move fast—they'll create roles for the right fit ✅ Remote-first is standard in VC-backed tech companies Pro tip: Set up Google Alerts for "[Your industry] Series A/B/C funding" and be the first to reach out. The best remote roles? They're never posted on LinkedIn. post_text: New from me in The Wall Street Journal: Landing a white-collar job is getting so tough that candidates—not companies—are paying recruiters to match them with positions. That has flipped the traditional recruiting model upside-down. Meet the "reverse recruiters": They find positions, customize resumes and even contact current employees. They can charge a set fee or a percentage of an applicant's starting salary once a job is accepted. Or both. But it points to how difficult the current world of online applications is to navigate — and how challenging it is to get a white-collar job right now. “If you are not paying, you are the product,” said Andre Hamra, Refer’s chief executive. “It incentivizes us to actually help the person.” At Reverse Recruiting Agency, Alex Shinkarovsky's team charges $1,500 monthly, plus a share of the first year's salary. He has 22 active clients. “Some folks just don’t have time to do it, some folks are scared, some folks are unemployed and on their last effort,” he said. More: https://lnkd.in/eWbw5DgY

In the traditional recruiting model, the candidate is still the product — presented, evaluated, and ultimately “purchased” by the employer. The *company* simply funds the search. It’s offer conversion.** Interviews can be generated. Offers remain market-driven decisions. Studies and articles describe this as an “arms race” or “doom loop” that makes hiring miserable and less human.

post_text: The number of Recruiters who cannot recruit beyond posting a job is honestly alarming. Companies are paying agency fees up to 30 percent of a Candidate’s annual salary and in many cases the hiring manager could have found that same person on LinkedIn in about ten minutes. Posting and praying is not recruiting. Real recruiting is identifying a market, mapping competitors, engaging passive Candidates, qualifying motivations, and managing both sides of the process from first conversation to acceptance. It is business development, relationship building, and influence. Not an Indeed notification. Large agency training used to create true Recruiters. People who knew how to open doors, run a search, and create value for a client. Somewhere along the way the model shifted to volume activity and software alerts. If your entire desk stops working when you do not have a job order to post, you do not have a recruiting business. You have a posting habit. Clients pay fees for access, insight, and control of the hiring process. When you actually recruit, you earn it and everyone wins. Experienced Recruiters who still believe in building a real desk know exactly what I am talking about.
comment_text: This is a very interesting topic to share and reflect on. I actually started in niche recruitment and experienced both sides of the industry. I began in a different era with in person interviews and large hiring drives, later transitioning into hybrid and high volume IT recruitment. At one point it became purely transactional and volume driven, which led me straight into burnout. Over time, I understood, recruiting is not about posting and waiting. It is about strategy, market mapping, competitive intelligence, understanding compensation, and being intentional about the clients and ecosystem you choose to operate in. It is also about networking with purpose and allowing yourself thinking time to analyze the market, refine your approach, and build real strategies instead of reacting. Patience is a powerful tool in this profession. Recruiting requires timing, discipline, and planning strategies. Today, working in retained executive search environment, the difference feels clear. When you operate in a true 360 full desk model, take ownership of business development, and specialize in a niche, something shifts. You start advising within a market. Recruiting is influence, intelligence, strategy, and discipline.

Put that same person in a high-pressure, timed whiteboard session on a random “Hard” dynamic programming problem… and yeah, there’s a real chance they don’t shine. Interview performance and real-world engineering impact are often completely different skill sets. post_text: This niche fire protection engineer got lowballed. He was promised $152K during the interview process. Then leadership stepped in: “We’ll offer $134K.” Recently, I was working with a large organisation on finding their next fire protection lead. This is a super niche role, and finding a fire protection engineer of this calibre is no small task. The talent pool is tight. The experience required is specific. And the right people aren’t actively applying for jobs. After months of searching, we finally found the guy. Perfect technical background. Strong leadership credibility. Available at the right time. The fire protection department manager met him, loved him, and they aligned on $152K. Handshake agreement. Everyone was on the same page. Then senior leadership reviewed the package. “We’re not comfortable at $152K. Let’s formalise at $134K.” We pushed back. Hard. But the response was: “We can’t disrupt our internal salary bandings for one hire.” When we went back to the candidate, his reaction was simple: “We already agreed terms. Why are we renegotiating?” I had to explain that the offer had been overridden internally. He walked. And I couldn’t blame him. This was a six-month search for an incredibly hard-to-fill fire protection position. In their justification, they benchmarked the role against other engineering disciplines, ignoring the fact that fire protection sits in its own market, with its own supply-and-demand pressures. On paper, it probably looked like they were saving $18K. In reality, they lost half a year of work and credibility with a well-connected professional in a tight-knit industry. When you’re hiring in fire protection, market rate isn’t a suggestion. It’s the cost of entry. Ignore it at your own cost.

post_text: One of the biggest pain points in the recruiting community? Recruiters can't get hired themselves. And the reasons? Wildly contradictory. Same recruiter. Same profile. Same experience. Company A → You're overqualified. Company B → You're underqualified. Company C → You haven't worked in our market. Company D → You've only done tech hiring. Company E → You've only done non-tech hiring. Company F → You don't have campus hiring experience. Company G → You haven't done GTM hiring before. Company H → You've never hired for leadership roles. Company I → You don't have volume hiring experience. Company J → You've only done niche hiring. And the list goes on… I'm sorry — how does this make sense? 🤔 The same person is too much for one and not enough for another? Think about what a recruiter actually does. Sourced. Screened. Convinced. Closed. For roles THEY have never personally done themselves. They figured out tech hiring without being a techie. They figured out niche markets without being a subject expert. They walked into the unknown and delivered. That IS the skill. So when an experienced recruiter applies to a new market why is that suddenly too big an ask? The irony is hard to ignore. We trust recruiters to judge talent every single day. But when THEY are the candidate, nothing is ever quite right. To every recruiter who has faced this 👇 Drop in the comments on how many of these reasons have you come across? What other rejection reasons have you faced? Let's get the full picture out here. At what point does experience stop being an asset and start becoming a reason to reject? post_text: “Estate agency is easy money” I hear it all the time. What people see: • A board goes up • A property goes online • It sells or lets • Commission gets paid What they don’t see: • Deals collapsing weeks before completion • Chains breaking • Late night negotiations • Viewings after hours • Difficult conversations about price • Managing emotions on both sides This job isn’t about opening doors. It’s managing risk, expectations, and problems while protecting clients from expensive mistakes. And here’s the truth most don’t realise: We only get paid if it works. No salary for “almost sold.” No commission for “nearly exchanged.” Good agents aren’t money hungry. They’re value driven. Because reputation travels fast in this industry, especially when you’re independent. #estateagentmyths #ukproperty #salesandlettings #realestate #propertyinsights

post_text: Everyone says that LinkedIn is the best platform for remote roles but I 100% disagree 👀 Don't get me wrong—LinkedIn is great. But if you're only applying to jobs here, you're missing the biggest opportunity. The hidden remote job market: VC-backed startups While everyone's refreshing LinkedIn Jobs and competing with 500+ applicants, there's a goldmine of opportunities hiding in plain sight. Here's what smart job seekers do: 1️⃣ Follow the money Head to Crunchbase or TechCrunch's funding roundups. Filter for companies that raised funding in the last 90 days. These startups just got capital to scale their teams—they NEED to hire, fast. 2️⃣ Get there before the job post Check their careers page and LinkedIn company profile. Read their funding announcement to understand their growth plans. Most haven't even written the job descriptions yet. 3️⃣ Reach out directly Message their Head of [Your Department] or hiring managers. Reference their recent funding round and explain how you can help them scale. You'll stand out because you did your homework. Why this approach wins: ✅ Zero competition (no job post = no applicants) ✅ Shows initiative and strategic thinking ✅ Startups move fast—they'll create roles for the right fit ✅ Remote-first is standard in VC-backed tech companies Pro tip: Set up Google Alerts for "[Your industry] Series A/B/C funding" and be the first to reach out. The best remote roles? They're never posted on LinkedIn. post_text: New from me in The Wall Street Journal: Landing a white-collar job is getting so tough that candidates—not companies—are paying recruiters to match them with positions. That has flipped the traditional recruiting model upside-down. Meet the "reverse recruiters": They find positions, customize resumes and even contact current employees. They can charge a set fee or a percentage of an applicant's starting salary once a job is accepted. Or both. But it points to how difficult the current world of online applications is to navigate — and how challenging it is to get a white-collar job right now. “If you are not paying, you are the product,” said Andre Hamra, Refer’s chief executive. “It incentivizes us to actually help the person.” At Reverse Recruiting Agency, Alex Shinkarovsky's team charges $1,500 monthly, plus a share of the first year's salary. comment_text: Reverse recruiting sounds reasonable on the surface. But letting someone else do the entire job search for you and outsourcing the thinking is concerning. There is no secret job database. Period. Many of these services imply they have access to hidden executive roles. What they are really talking about is access through privilege. The so called hidden job market often benefits people who already have social capital, status, or insider networks. That opens the door to bias and directly undermines DEI. If entry to opportunity requires paying for access, then the system is already broken. To be clear, I am not questioning how much people choose to invest. I am questioning the idea of outsourcing the whole job search. Jobseekers need more than placements. They need skills, strategy, and confidence to navigate the market on their own. What works once should work again later in their career. That is the part too many services skip. Lindsay

comment_text: A major driver no one names is age discrimination. Companies fear hiring someone who “might retire in five years,” yet the younger hires they choose often leave within 18–36 months. The fear doesn’t match reality. For anyone unemployed long‑term, paying a recruiter $1,500 a month — plus a percentage of their first‑year salary — is punishing. People are doing everything they can to stay afloat, while corporations seeking “highly skilled talent” pay nothing. That doesn’t feel empowering. It feels dystopian. And the ghosting exposes the dysfunction. Candidates are told they’re “top contenders,” then never hear another word. When they follow up, it’s crickets. Ghosting isn’t a hiring strategy. It’s unprofessional. If you’re seriously hiring, you know how to send a simple, respectful update: “Thank you for your time — this position has been filled.” The market doesn’t need more paid gatekeepers. It needs hiring teams who value experience, communicate like adults, and stop treating seasoned talent like a liability.

comment_text: There’s a subtle economic nuance embedded in the “who is the product” framing. In the traditional recruiting model, the candidate is still the product — presented, evaluated, and ultimately “purchased” by the employer. The *company* simply funds the search. Reverse recruiting doesn’t eliminate that dynamic. It shifts **who pays for representation,** not who functions as the asset being matched. Which makes this trend read much more like a talent-agent model — similar to what we see in professional sports. ✅ Recruiters resemble scouts working for **the team** (company). 🔺 Reverse recruiters resemble **agents** working for **the player** (candidate). That distinction matters because it changes expectations. ◀️ Especially at the leadership level, the meaningful success metric isn’t interview volume. It’s offer conversion.** Interviews can be generated. Offers remain market-driven decisions. comment_text: AI has flooded the system on both ends: Job seekers widely use tools like ChatGPT to generate resumes, cover letters, and even interview prep (often 60-90% of applicants in surveys). This creates a massive volume of applications…many generic or “AI-optimized” for keyword matching in applicant tracking systems (ATS). post_text: The 2–4 year engineer isn’t junior. It’s prime. And it’s the most competitive hire in engineering and manufacturing right now. You want someone who: • Already has real project reps • Understands production pressure • Can contribute without hand-holding • Still has upside • Isn’t priced like a senior That’s not entry-level. That’s premium early-career talent. And every company is hunting the same profile. So when you say, “We just need someone with 2–4 years…” You’re stepping into one of the most competitive talent battles in the market. These engineers aren’t hoping. They’re choosing. Multiple interviews. Multiple offers. Offers accepted before some teams finish debating. If you’re targeting 2–4 year engineers, you’re not hiring junior talent. You’re competing for prime talent. Are you hiring like it?

post_text: The number of Recruiters who cannot recruit beyond posting a job is honestly alarming. It is business development, relationship building, and influence. Not an Indeed notification. Large agency training used to create true Recruiters. People who knew how to open doors, run a search, and create value for a client. Somewhere along the way the model shifted to volume activity and software alerts. If your entire desk stops working when you do not have a job order to post, you do not have a recruiting business. You have a posting habit. Clients pay fees for access, insight, and control of the hiring process. When you actually recruit, you earn it and everyone wins. Recruiting is influence, intelligence, strategy, and discipline.

comment_text: I call it the "1986 Toyota Corolla Problem" Imagine turning down a seasoned cross-country driver because they haven't specifically driven a Toyota Corolla. Sounds ridiculous, right? Yet, this is exactly what happens in IT hiring every day. Hiring managers and teams get so hyper-focused on whether a candidate has used one specific, niche tool or framework that they completely miss the bigger picture. Instead of asking, "Have you driven this exact car?" we need to be asking: "How many miles have you driven?" "Do you know how to drive a manual?" "Do you know how to read the owner's manual?" Technology changes constantly. The specific "car" your team is driving today probably won't be the one you're driving in three years. If someone is a great driver who understands the mechanics of the road and knows how to read the manual, they can drive your tech stack. Let's stop hiring for matching acronyms on a resume and start hiring for adaptability, fundamentals, and problem-solving mileage.

comment_text: In many hiring processes, especially in technical roles, coding tests are often presented as objective measures of skill. However, in reality, they are sometimes used more as filtering tools than as true evaluations of ability. Hiring decisions are frequently influenced by subjective factors. If an interviewer likes a candidate, they may be more willing to overlook gaps in knowledge and provide training on the job. On the other hand, if they feel a disconnect for any reason, technical assessments can become a convenient justification for rejection. In practice, factors such as personal bias, cultural fit, background, race, gender, religion, or perceived “roots” can influence hiring decisions—whether consciously or unconsciously. While technical skills matter, they are not always the sole or even primary factor in who ultimately gets hired.

post_text: This niche fire protection engineer got lowballed. He was promised $152K during the interview process. Then leadership stepped in: “We’ll offer $134K.” Recently, I was working with a large organisation on finding their next fire protection lead. This is a super niche role, and finding a fire protection engineer of this calibre is no small task. The talent pool is tight. The experience required is specific. And the right people aren’t actively applying for jobs. After months of searching, we finally found the guy. Perfect technical background. Strong leadership credibility. Available at the right time. The fire protection department manager met him, loved him, and they aligned on $152K. Handshake agreement. Everyone was on the same page. Then senior leadership reviewed the package. “We’re not comfortable at $152K. Let’s formalise at $134K.” We pushed back. Hard. But the response was: “We can’t disrupt our internal salary bandings for one hire.” When we went back to the candidate, his reaction was simple: “We already agreed terms. Why are we renegotiating?” I had to explain that the offer had been overridden internally. He walked. And I couldn’t blame him. This was a six-month search for an incredibly hard-to-fill fire protection position. In their justification, they benchmarked the role against other engineering disciplines, ignoring the fact that fire protection sits in its own market, with its own supply-and-demand pressures. On paper, it probably looked like they were saving $18K. In reality, they lost half a year of work and credibility with a well-connected professional in a tight-knit industry. When you’re hiring in fire protection, market rate isn’t a suggestion. It’s the cost of entry. Ignore it at your own cost.

Then leadership stepped in: “We’ll offer $134K.” Recently, I was working with a large organisation on finding their next fire protection lead. This is a super niche role, and finding a fire protection engineer of this calibre is no small task. The talent pool is tight. The experience required is specific. And the right people aren’t actively applying for jobs. After months of searching, we finally found the guy. Perfect technical background. Strong leadership credibility. Available at the right time. The fire protection department manager met him, loved him, and they aligned on $152K. Handshake agreement. Everyone was on the same page. Then senior leadership reviewed the package. “We’re not comfortable at $152K. Let’s formalise at $134K.” We pushed back. Hard. But the response was: “We can’t disrupt our internal salary bandings for one hire.” When we went back to the candidate, his reaction was simple: “We already agreed terms. Why are we renegotiating?” I had to explain that the offer had been overridden internally. He walked. And I couldn’t blame him. This was a six-month search for an incredibly hard-to-fill fire protection position. In their justification, they benchmarked the role against other engineering disciplines, ignoring the fact that fire protection sits in its own market, with its own supply-and-demand pressures. On paper, it probably looked like they were saving $18K. In reality, they lost half a year of work and credibility with a well-connected professional in a tight-knit industry. When you’re hiring in fire protection, market rate isn’t a suggestion. It’s the cost of entry. Ignore it at your own cost.

post_text: One of the biggest pain points in the recruiting community? Recruiters can't get hired themselves. And the reasons? Wildly contradictory. Same recruiter. Same profile. Same experience. Company A → You're overqualified. Company B → You're underqualified. Company C → You haven't worked in our market. Company D → You've only done tech hiring. Company E → You've only done non-tech hiring. Company F → You don't have campus hiring experience. Company G → You haven't done GTM hiring before. Company H → You've never hired for leadership roles. Company I → You don't have volume hiring experience. Company J → You've only done niche hiring. And the list goes on… I'm sorry — how does this make sense? 🤔 The same person is too much for one and not enough for another? Think about what a recruiter actually does. Sourced. Screened. Convinced. Closed. For roles THEY have never personally done themselves. They figured out tech hiring without being a techie. They figured out niche markets without being a subject expert. They walked into the unknown and delivered. That IS the skill. So when an experienced recruiter applies to a new market why is that suddenly too big an ask? The irony is hard to ignore. We trust recruiters to judge talent every single day. But when THEY are the candidate, nothing is ever quite right. To every recruiter who has faced this 👇 Drop in the comments on how many of these reasons have you come across? What other rejection reasons have you faced? Let's get the full picture out here. At what point does experience stop being an asset and start becoming a reason to reject? Genuine question. #Recruiting #TalentAcquisition #HiringManagers #RecruiterLife #HR #RecruitersOfLinkedIn #HiringBias #JobSearch #FutureOfWork #HumanResources

Company A → You're overqualified. Company B → You're underqualified. Company C → You haven't worked in our market. Company D → You've only done tech hiring. Company I → You don't have volume hiring experience. Company J → You've only done niche hiring. Closed. For roles THEY have never personally done themselves. They figured out tech hiring without being a techie. They figured out niche markets without being a subject expert. They walked into the unknown and delivered. That IS the skill. So when an experienced recruiter applies to a new market why is that suddenly too big an ask? The irony is hard to ignore. We trust recruiters to judge talent every single day. But when THEY are the candidate, nothing is ever quite right. If we hire 67% fewer juniors in 2024-2026, we'll have 67% fewer mid-level developers in 2027-2029. And 67% fewer senior developers in 2031-2033. Every company wants senior engineers. comment_text: The junior market is tighter. That’s real. But I’m not convinced this is purely an AI story. Entry-level roles are always the most elastic during downturns. We saw similar contractions after the dot-com bust and 2008. Juniors are the easiest lever to pull when companies de-risk. The more interesting question is long-term pipeline dynamics. If we suppress entry for multiple years, mid-level scarcity becomes inevitable. Markets tend to correct scarcity. The real shift may not be elimination of juniors, but a redefinition of what “entry-level” looks like in an AI-augmented workflow. I’m curious whether this is structural displacement or cyclical contraction amplified by new tooling.

comment_text: I’ve never worked at the big tech companies like Microsoft or Amazon. Hopefully they have a strong concentration of good engineers. However, in many regular companies, it’s clear that a large portion of developers, easily 50% in typical teams and closer to 80% in many offshore shops, can now be handled by Claude or Copilot. A lot of people entered software for the high salaries and low barriers, not because they cared about architecture, systems thinking, or improving the product. They don’t understand the “what” or the “why,” and they expect every task to be fully spelled out in a sprint ticket. That kind of work is exactly what LLM agents are good at. The juniors and seniors who actually care about the craft will do well. Developers who understand the system they’re building, not just the syntax, will remain valuable. Well defined, repetitive tasks can be outsourced to an LLM now, but the thinking and reasoning behind the system still require real engineers.

post_text: Everyone says that LinkedIn is the best platform for remote roles but I 100% disagree 👀 Don't get me wrong—LinkedIn is great. But if you're only applying to jobs here, you're missing the biggest opportunity. The hidden remote job market: VC-backed startups While everyone's refreshing LinkedIn Jobs and competing with 500+ applicants, there's a goldmine of opportunities hiding in plain sight. Here's what smart job seekers do: 1️⃣ Follow the money Head to Crunchbase or TechCrunch's funding roundups. Filter for companies that raised funding in the last 90 days. These startups just got capital to scale their teams—they NEED to hire, fast. 2️⃣ Get there before the job post Check their careers page and LinkedIn company profile. Read their funding announcement to understand their growth plans. Most haven't even written the job descriptions yet. 3️⃣ Reach out directly Message their Head of [Your Department] or hiring managers. Reference their recent funding round and explain how you can help them scale. You'll stand out because you did your homework. Why this approach wins: ✅ Zero competition (no job post = no applicants) ✅ Shows initiative and strategic thinking ✅ Startups move fast—they'll create roles for the right fit ✅ Remote-first is standard in VC-backed tech companies Pro tip: Set up Google Alerts for "[Your industry] Series A/B/C funding" and be the first to reach out. The best remote roles? They're never posted on LinkedIn. post_text: Everyone says that LinkedIn is the best platform for remote roles but I 100% disagree 👀 Don't get me wrong—LinkedIn is great. But if you're only applying to jobs here, you're missing the biggest opportunity. The hidden remote job market: VC-backed startups While everyone's refreshing LinkedIn Jobs and competing with 500+ applicants, there's a goldmine of opportunities hiding in plain sight. Here's what smart job seekers do: 1️⃣ Follow the money Head to Crunchbase or TechCrunch's funding roundups. Filter for companies that raised funding in the last 90 days. These startups just got capital to scale their teams—they NEED to hire, fast. 2️⃣ Get there before the job post Check their careers page and LinkedIn company profile. Read their funding announcement to understand their growth plans. Most haven't even written the job descriptions yet. 3️⃣ Reach out directly Message their Head of [Your Department] or hiring managers. Reference their recent funding round and explain how you can help them scale. You'll stand out because you did your homework. Why this approach wins: ✅ Zero competition (no job post = no applicants) ✅ Shows initiative and strategic thinking ✅ Startups move fast—they'll create roles for the right fit ✅ Remote-first is standard in VC-backed tech companies Pro tip: Set up Google Alerts for "[Your industry] Series A/B/C funding" and be the first to reach out. The best remote roles? They're never posted on LinkedIn. post_text: New from me in The Wall Street Journal: Landing a white-collar job is getting so tough that candidates—not companies—are paying recruiters to match them with positions. That has flipped the traditional recruiting model upside-down. Meet the "reverse recruiters": They find positions, customize resumes and even contact current employees. They can charge a set fee or a percentage of an applicant's starting salary once a job is accepted. Or both. But it points to how difficult the current world of online applications is to navigate — and how challenging it is to get a white-collar job right now. “If you are not paying, you are the product,” said Andre Hamra, Refer’s chief executive. “It incentivizes us to actually help the person.” At Reverse Recruiting Agency, Alex Shinkarovsky's team charges $1,500 monthly, plus a share of the first year's salary. He has 22 active clients. “Some folks just don’t have time to do it, some folks are scared, some folks are unemployed and on their last effort,” he said. More: https://lnkd.in/eWbw5DgY

comment_text: There’s a subtle economic nuance embedded in the “who is the product” framing. In the traditional recruiting model, the candidate is still the product — presented, evaluated, and ultimately “purchased” by the employer. The *company* simply funds the search. Reverse recruiting doesn’t eliminate that dynamic. It shifts **who pays for representation,** not who functions as the asset being matched. Which makes this trend read much more like a talent-agent model — similar to what we see in professional sports. ✅ Recruiters resemble scouts working for **the team** (company). 🔺 Reverse recruiters resemble **agents** working for **the player** (candidate). That distinction matters because it changes expectations. ◀️ Especially at the leadership level, the meaningful success metric isn’t interview volume. It’s offer conversion.** Interviews can be generated. Offers remain market-driven decisions. I cover the "talent agent" vs "talent scout" model in a Forbes Coaches Council article, Feb 2024. https://www.forbes.com/councils/forbescoachescouncil/2024/02/21/will-an-executive-recruiter-find-a-job-for-me-3-recruitment-models-and-how-to-leverage-relationships-with-recruiters/

post_text: The 2–4 year engineer isn’t junior. It’s prime. And it’s the most competitive hire in engineering and manufacturing right now. You want someone who: • Already has real project reps • Understands production pressure • Can contribute without hand-holding • Still has upside • Isn’t priced like a senior That’s not entry-level. That’s premium early-career talent. And every company is hunting the same profile. So when you say, “We just need someone with 2–4 years…” You’re stepping into one of the most competitive talent battles in the market. These engineers aren’t hoping. They’re choosing. Multiple interviews. Multiple offers. Offers accepted before some teams finish debating. If you’re targeting 2–4 year engineers, you’re not hiring junior talent. You’re competing for prime talent. Are you hiring like it?

post_text: Most startups don’t fail because of the product. They fail because of their first leadership hire. I’ve seen this pattern over and over again. Founders hire too fast. They hire on vibes. post_text: The number of Recruiters who cannot recruit beyond posting a job is honestly alarming. Companies are paying agency fees up to 30 percent of a Candidate’s annual salary and in many cases the hiring manager could have found that same person on LinkedIn in about ten minutes. Posting and praying is not recruiting. Real recruiting is identifying a market, mapping competitors, engaging passive Candidates, qualifying motivations, and managing both sides of the process from first conversation to acceptance. It is business development, relationship building, and influence. Not an Indeed notification. Large agency training used to create true Recruiters. People who knew how to open doors, run a search, and create value for a client. Somewhere along the way the model shifted to volume activity and software alerts. If your entire desk stops working when you do not have a job order to post, you do not have a recruiting business. You have a posting habit. Clients pay fees for access, insight, and control of the hiring process. When you actually recruit, you earn it and everyone wins. Experienced Recruiters who still believe in building a real desk know exactly what I am talking about.
comment_text: This resonates. 11+ years in agency recruiting and business development taught me that real recruiting was never “post and pray.” It was market mapping, competitor analysis, passive outreach, and relationship building long before a job order ever hit the desk. I do think COVID accelerated a major shift. Many experienced headhunters exited the industry, teams downsized, and volume became the priority over strategy. At the same time, many organizations became heavily dependent on AI tools, resume scanning, automated rejections, workflow automation, which increased efficiency but reduced human interaction. AI should enhance recruiting, not replace discernment. When algorithms filter before a recruiter even reviews a profile, you risk missing high-potential talent. And when recruiters are buried in back-to-back meetings and administrative tasks, they don’t have the time to truly headhunt. That’s not an individual failure it’s often structural.The best recruiters still build pipelines before they’re needed. They still strategically source. They take time to study each role deeply and create intentional hiring plans. They continuously build strong relationships with candidates and clients not just when there’s an opening, but always.

Yet, this is exactly what happens in IT hiring every day. Hiring managers and teams get so hyper-focused on whether a candidate has used one specific, niche tool or framework that they completely miss the bigger picture. Instead of asking, "Have you driven this exact car?" we need to be asking: "How many miles have you driven?" "Do you know how to drive a manual?" "Do you know how to read the owner's manual?" Technology changes constantly. The specific "car" your team is driving today probably won't be the one you're driving in three years. If someone is a great driver who understands the mechanics of the road and knows how to read the manual, they can drive your tech stack. Let's stop hiring for matching acronyms on a resume and start hiring for adaptability, fundamentals, and problem-solving mileage.

comment_text: In many hiring processes, especially in technical roles, coding tests are often presented as objective measures of skill. However, in reality, they are sometimes used more as filtering tools than as true evaluations of ability. Hiring decisions are frequently influenced by subjective factors. If an interviewer likes a candidate, they may be more willing to overlook gaps in knowledge and provide training on the job. post_text: This niche fire protection engineer got lowballed. He was promised $152K during the interview process. Then leadership stepped in: “We’ll offer $134K.” Recently, I was working with a large organisation on finding their next fire protection lead. This is a super niche role, and finding a fire protection engineer of this calibre is no small task. The talent pool is tight. The experience required is specific. And the right people aren’t actively applying for jobs. After months of searching, we finally found the guy. Perfect technical background. Strong leadership credibility. Available at the right time. The fire protection department manager met him, loved him, and they aligned on $152K. Handshake agreement. Everyone was on the same page. Then senior leadership reviewed the package. “We’re not comfortable at $152K. Let’s formalise at $134K.” We pushed back. Hard. But the response was: “We can’t disrupt our internal salary bandings for one hire.” When we went back to the candidate, his reaction was simple: “We already agreed terms. post_text: One of the biggest pain points in the recruiting community? Recruiters can't get hired themselves. And the reasons? Wildly contradictory. Same recruiter. Same profile. Same experience. Company A → You're overqualified. Company B → You're underqualified. Company C → You haven't worked in our market. Company D → You've only done tech hiring. Company E → You've only done non-tech hiring. Company F → You don't have campus hiring experience. Company G → You haven't done GTM hiring before. Company H → You've never hired for leadership roles. Company I → You don't have volume hiring experience. Company J → You've only done niche hiring. And the list goes on… I'm sorry — how does this make sense? 🤔 The same person is too much for one and not enough for another? Think about what a recruiter actually does. Sourced. Screened. Convinced. Closed. For roles THEY have never personally done themselves. They figured out tech hiring without being a techie. They figured out niche markets without being a subject expert. They walked into the unknown and delivered. That IS the skill. So when an experienced recruiter applies to a new market why is that suddenly too big an ask? The irony is hard to ignore. We trust recruiters to judge talent every single day. But when THEY are the candidate, nothing is ever quite right. To every recruiter who has faced this 👇 Drop in the comments on how many of these reasons have you come across? What other rejection reasons have you faced? Let's get the full picture out here. At what point does experience stop being an asset and start becoming a reason to reject? Company I → You don't have volume hiring experience. Company J → You've only done niche hiring. And the list goes on… I'm sorry — how does this make sense? 🤔 The same person is too much for one and not enough for another? Think about what a recruiter actually does. Sourced. Screened. Convinced. Closed. For roles THEY have never personally done themselves. They figured out tech hiring without being a techie. They figured out niche markets without being a subject expert. They walked into the unknown and delivered. That IS the skill. So when an experienced recruiter applies to a new market why is that suddenly too big an ask? The irony is hard to ignore. We trust recruiters to judge talent every single day. But when THEY are the candidate, nothing is ever quite right. post_text: “We can’t find skilled tradespeople.” Translation: “We posted the job, waited three weeks, offered 2019 wages… and now we’re confused.” Let’s be honest for a second. The labor market didn’t disappear. It evolved. Right now: • Welders know exactly what the shop down the street is paying. • Maintenance techs compare overtime structures like fantasy football stats. • Engineers won’t wait 4 weeks for a second interview. • The best foremen are recruited before their boots hit the parking lot. And yet some companies are still hiring like it’s 2008. My favorite is: “Must have 10 years of experience, be proficient in everything, willing to work weekends… budget is tight though.” That’s not a job description. That’s a unicorn hunting expedition. 🦄 Here’s what’s actually working in skilled trades & engineering staffing right now: ✔ Fast interview processes (days, not weeks) ✔ Clear pay ranges (no mystery math) ✔ Overtime transparency ✔ Safe, well-managed projects ✔ Leaders who actually lead The companies winning aren’t lucky. They’re realistic. They understand that tradespeople and engineers are professionals — not line items. If you’re still blaming a “talent shortage,” it might be time to audit your hiring process… not the workforce. #SkilledTrades #EngineeringJobs #ConstructionHiring #ManufacturingCareers #StaffingIndustry #WorkforceReality

Read their funding announcement to understand their growth plans. Reference their recent funding round and explain how you can help them scale. You'll stand out because you did your homework. Why this approach wins: ✅ Zero competition (no job post = no applicants) ✅ Shows initiative and strategic thinking ✅ Startups move fast—they'll create roles for the right fit ✅ Remote-first is standard in VC-backed tech companies Pro tip: Set up Google Alerts for "[Your industry] Series A/B/C funding" and be the first to reach out. The best remote roles? They're never posted on LinkedIn. comment_text: Reverse recruiting sounds reasonable on the surface. But letting someone else do the entire job search for you and outsourcing the thinking is concerning. There is no secret job database. Period. Many of these services imply they have access to hidden executive roles. What they are really talking about is access through privilege. The so called hidden job market often benefits people who already have social capital, status, or insider networks. That opens the door to bias and directly undermines DEI. If entry to opportunity requires paying for access, then the system is already broken. To be clear, I am not questioning how much people choose to invest. I am questioning the idea of outsourcing the whole job search. Jobseekers need more than placements. They need skills, strategy, and confidence to navigate the market on their own. What works once should work again later in their career. That is the part too many services skip. Lindsay

post_text: The number of Recruiters who cannot recruit beyond posting a job is honestly alarming. Companies are paying agency fees up to 30 percent of a Candidate’s annual salary and in many cases the hiring manager could have found that same person on LinkedIn in about ten minutes. Posting and praying is not recruiting. Real recruiting is identifying a market, mapping competitors, engaging passive Candidates, qualifying motivations, and managing both sides of the process from first conversation to acceptance. It is business development, relationship building, and influence. Not an Indeed notification. Large agency training used to create true Recruiters. People who knew how to open doors, run a search, and create value for a client. Somewhere along the way the model shifted to volume activity and software alerts. If your entire desk stops working when you do not have a job order to post, you do not have a recruiting business. You have a posting habit. Clients pay fees for access, insight, and control of the hiring process. When you actually recruit, you earn it and everyone wins. Experienced Recruiters who still believe in building a real desk know exactly what I am talking about.

If someone is a great driver who understands the mechanics of the road and knows how to read the manual, they can drive your tech stack. Let's stop hiring for matching acronyms on a resume and start hiring for adaptability, fundamentals, and problem-solving mileage.

post_text: This niche fire protection engineer got lowballed. He was promised $152K during the interview process. Then leadership stepped in: “We’ll offer $134K.” Recently, I was working with a large organisation on finding their next fire protection lead. This is a super niche role, and finding a fire protection engineer of this calibre is no small task. The talent pool is tight. The experience required is specific. And the right people aren’t actively applying for jobs. After months of searching, we finally found the guy. Perfect technical background. Strong leadership credibility. Available at the right time. The fire protection department manager met him, loved him, and they aligned on $152K. Handshake agreement. Everyone was on the same page. Then senior leadership reviewed the package. “We’re not comfortable at $152K. Let’s formalise at $134K.” We pushed back. Hard. But the response was: “We can’t disrupt our internal salary bandings for one hire.” When we went back to the candidate, his reaction was simple: “We already agreed terms. Why are we renegotiating?” I had to explain that the offer had been overridden internally. He walked. And I couldn’t blame him. This was a six-month search for an incredibly hard-to-fill fire protection position. In their justification, they benchmarked the role against other engineering disciplines, ignoring the fact that fire protection sits in its own market, with its own supply-and-demand pressures. On paper, it probably looked like they were saving $18K. In reality, they lost half a year of work and credibility with a well-connected professional in a tight-knit industry. When you’re hiring in fire protection, market rate isn’t a suggestion. It’s the cost of entry. Ignore it at your own cost.

post_text: One of the biggest pain points in the recruiting community? Recruiters can't get hired themselves. And the reasons? Wildly contradictory. Same recruiter. Same profile. Same experience. Company A → You're overqualified. Company B → You're underqualified. Company C → You haven't worked in our market. Company D → You've only done tech hiring. Company E → You've only done non-tech hiring. Company F → You don't have campus hiring experience. Company G → You haven't done GTM hiring before. Company H → You've never hired for leadership roles. Company I → You don't have volume hiring experience. Company J → You've only done niche hiring. And the list goes on… I'm sorry — how does this make sense? 🤔 The same person is too much for one and not enough for another? Think about what a recruiter actually does. Sourced. Screened. Convinced. Closed. For roles THEY have never personally done themselves. They figured out tech hiring without being a techie. They figured out niche markets without being a subject expert. They walked into the unknown and delivered. That IS the skill. So when an experienced recruiter applies to a new market why is that suddenly too big an ask? The irony is hard to ignore. We trust recruiters to judge talent every single day. But when THEY are the candidate, nothing is ever quite right. To every recruiter who has faced this 👇 Drop in the comments on how many of these reasons have you come across? What other rejection reasons have you faced? Let's get the full picture out here. At what point does experience stop being an asset and start becoming a reason to reject? Genuine question. #Recruiting #TalentAcquisition #HiringManagers #RecruiterLife #HR #RecruitersOfLinkedIn #HiringBias #JobSearch #FutureOfWork #HumanResources

No salary for “almost sold.” No commission for “nearly exchanged.” Good agents aren’t money hungry. They’re value driven. Because reputation travels fast in this industry, especially when you’re independent. #estateagentmyths #ukproperty #salesandlettings #realestate #propertyinsights

post_text: Everyone says that LinkedIn is the best platform for remote roles but I 100% disagree 👀 Don't get me wrong—LinkedIn is great. But if you're only applying to jobs here, you're missing the biggest opportunity. The hidden remote job market: VC-backed startups While everyone's refreshing LinkedIn Jobs and competing with 500+ applicants, there's a goldmine of opportunities hiding in plain sight. Here's what smart job seekers do: 1️⃣ Follow the money Head to Crunchbase or TechCrunch's funding roundups. Filter for companies that raised funding in the last 90 days. These startups just got capital to scale their teams—they NEED to hire, fast. 2️⃣ Get there before the job post Check their careers page and LinkedIn company profile. Read their funding announcement to understand their growth plans. Most haven't even written the job descriptions yet. 3️⃣ Reach out directly Message their Head of [Your Department] or hiring managers. Reference their recent funding round and explain how you can help them scale. You'll stand out because you did your homework. Why this approach wins: ✅ Zero competition (no job post = no applicants) ✅ Shows initiative and strategic thinking ✅ Startups move fast—they'll create roles for the right fit ✅ Remote-first is standard in VC-backed tech companies Pro tip: Set up Google Alerts for "[Your industry] Series A/B/C funding" and be the first to reach out. The best remote roles? They're never posted on LinkedIn. comment_text: There’s a subtle economic nuance embedded in the “who is the product” framing. In the traditional recruiting model, the candidate is still the product — presented, evaluated, and ultimately “purchased” by the employer. The *company* simply funds the search. Reverse recruiting doesn’t eliminate that dynamic. It shifts **who pays for representation,** not who functions as the asset being matched. Which makes this trend read much more like a talent-agent model — similar to what we see in professional sports. ✅ Recruiters resemble scouts working for **the team** (company). 🔺 Reverse recruiters resemble **agents** working for **the player** (candidate). comment_text: AI has flooded the system on both ends: Job seekers widely use tools like ChatGPT to generate resumes, cover letters, and even interview prep (often 60-90% of applicants in surveys). This creates a massive volume of applications…many generic or “AI-optimized” for keyword matching in applicant tracking systems (ATS). Recruiters and companies respond by tightening AI filters, adding more screening layers, or ghosting more aggressively to cope with the noise. The result is a vicious cycle: more applications…worse signal-to-noise...longer searches, higher rejection rates, and widespread frustration. Studies and articles describe this as an “arms race” or “doom loop” that makes hiring miserable and less human.

There are reputable ways people can help job seekers and get paid, but I cringe at what I hear is 'new' as I realize it's not. Also, I created an all-free job search process with resources at www.JobSeeker.Training as I actually want to help people versus monetize them. post_text: The 2–4 year engineer isn’t junior. It’s prime. And it’s the most competitive hire in engineering and manufacturing right now. You want someone who: • Already has real project reps • Understands production pressure • Can contribute without hand-holding • Still has upside • Isn’t priced like a senior That’s not entry-level. That’s premium early-career talent. And every company is hunting the same profile. So when you say, “We just need someone with 2–4 years…” You’re stepping into one of the most competitive talent battles in the market. These engineers aren’t hoping. They’re choosing. Multiple interviews. Multiple offers. Offers accepted before some teams finish debating. If you’re targeting 2–4 year engineers, you’re not hiring junior talent. You’re competing for prime talent. Are you hiring like it?

post_text: The number of Recruiters who cannot recruit beyond posting a job is honestly alarming. Companies are paying agency fees up to 30 percent of a Candidate’s annual salary and in many cases the hiring manager could have found that same person on LinkedIn in about ten minutes. Posting and praying is not recruiting. Real recruiting is identifying a market, mapping competitors, engaging passive Candidates, qualifying motivations, and managing both sides of the process from first conversation to acceptance. It is business development, relationship building, and influence. Not an Indeed notification. Large agency training used to create true Recruiters. People who knew how to open doors, run a search, and create value for a client. Somewhere along the way the model shifted to volume activity and software alerts. If your entire desk stops working when you do not have a job order to post, you do not have a recruiting business. You have a posting habit. Clients pay fees for access, insight, and control of the hiring process. When you actually recruit, you earn it and everyone wins. Experienced Recruiters who still believe in building a real desk know exactly what I am talking about.
comment_text: This is a very interesting topic to share and reflect on. I actually started in niche recruitment and experienced both sides of the industry. I began in a different era with in person interviews and large hiring drives, later transitioning into hybrid and high volume IT recruitment. At one point it became purely transactional and volume driven, which led me straight into burnout. Over time, I understood, recruiting is not about posting and waiting. It is about strategy, market mapping, competitive intelligence, understanding compensation, and being intentional about the clients and ecosystem you choose to operate in. It is also about networking with purpose and allowing yourself thinking time to analyze the market, refine your approach, and build real strategies instead of reacting. Patience is a powerful tool in this profession. Recruiting requires timing, discipline, and planning strategies. Today, working in retained executive search environment, the difference feels clear. When you operate in a true 360 full desk model, take ownership of business development, and specialize in a niche, something shifts. You start advising within a market. Recruiting is influence, intelligence, strategy, and discipline.

I do think COVID accelerated a major shift. Many experienced headhunters exited the industry, teams downsized, and volume became the priority over strategy. And when recruiters are buried in back-to-back meetings and administrative tasks, they don’t have the time to truly headhunt. That’s not an individual failure it’s often structural.The best recruiters still build pipelines before they’re needed. They still strategically source. They take time to study each role deeply and create intentional hiring plans. They continuously build strong relationships with candidates and clients not just when there’s an opening, but always.

Interview performance and real-world engineering impact are often completely different skill sets. Great engineers: Make pragmatic trade-offs under uncertainty Write maintainable code that survives years, not minutes Communicate clearly across teams Reduce long-term complexity instead of optimizing for cleverness Most technical interviews, on the other hand, optimize for speed, pattern recognition, and performance under artificial pressure. That doesn’t mean algorithmic thinking isn’t valuable — it absolutely is. But if that’s the primary filter, we may be systematically screening out the very people who would become force multipliers inside the organization. The real question is powerful: if our process doesn’t measure what makes our best engineers great, what signal are we actually selecting for? Unpopular? Maybe. Necessary conversation? Definitely.
