comment_text: I call it the "1986 Toyota Corolla Problem" Imagine turning down a seasoned cross-country driver because they haven't specifically driven a Toyota Corolla. Sounds ridiculous, right? Yet, this is exactly what happens in IT hiring every day. Hiring managers and teams get so hyper-focused on whether a candidate has used one specific, niche tool or framework that they completely miss the bigger picture. Instead of asking, "Have you driven this exact car?" we need to be asking: "How many miles have you driven?" "Do you know how to drive a manual?" "Do you know how to read the owner's manual?" Technology changes constantly. The specific "car" your team is driving today probably won't be the one you're driving in three years. If someone is a great driver who understands the mechanics of the road and knows how to read the manual, they can drive your tech stack. Let's stop hiring for matching acronyms on a resume and start hiring for adaptability, fundamentals, and problem-solving mileage.

comment_text: There’s a subtle economic nuance embedded in the “who is the product” framing. In the traditional recruiting model, the candidate is still the product — presented, evaluated, and ultimately “purchased” by the employer. The *company* simply funds the search. Reverse recruiting doesn’t eliminate that dynamic. It shifts **who pays for representation,** not who functions as the asset being matched. Which makes this trend read much more like a talent-agent model — similar to what we see in professional sports. ✅ Recruiters resemble scouts working for **the team** (company). 🔺 Reverse recruiters resemble **agents** working for **the player** (candidate). That distinction matters because it changes expectations. ◀️ Especially at the leadership level, the meaningful success metric isn’t interview volume. It’s offer conversion.** Interviews can be generated. Offers remain market-driven decisions. I cover the "talent agent" vs "talent scout" model in a Forbes Coaches Council article, Feb 2024. https://www.forbes.com/councils/forbescoachescouncil/2024/02/21/will-an-executive-recruiter-find-a-job-for-me-3-recruitment-models-and-how-to-leverage-relationships-with-recruiters/

comment_text: A major driver no one names is age discrimination. Companies fear hiring someone who “might retire in five years,” yet the younger hires they choose often leave within 18–36 months. The fear doesn’t match reality. For anyone unemployed long‑term, paying a recruiter $1,500 a month — plus a percentage of their first‑year salary — is punishing. People are doing everything they can to stay afloat, while corporations seeking “highly skilled talent” pay nothing. That doesn’t feel empowering. It feels dystopian. And the ghosting exposes the dysfunction. Candidates are told they’re “top contenders,” then never hear another word. When they follow up, it’s crickets. Ghosting isn’t a hiring strategy. It’s unprofessional. If you’re seriously hiring, you know how to send a simple, respectful update: “Thank you for your time — this position has been filled.” The market doesn’t need more paid gatekeepers. It needs hiring teams who value experience, communicate like adults, and stop treating seasoned talent like a liability.

post_text: The number of Recruiters who cannot recruit beyond posting a job is honestly alarming. Companies are paying agency fees up to 30 percent of a Candidate’s annual salary and in many cases the hiring manager could have found that same person on LinkedIn in about ten minutes. Posting and praying is not recruiting. Real recruiting is identifying a market, mapping competitors, engaging passive Candidates, qualifying motivations, and managing both sides of the process from first conversation to acceptance. It is business development, relationship building, and influence. Not an Indeed notification. Large agency training used to create true Recruiters. People who knew how to open doors, run a search, and create value for a client. Somewhere along the way the model shifted to volume activity and software alerts. If your entire desk stops working when you do not have a job order to post, you do not have a recruiting business. You have a posting habit. Clients pay fees for access, insight, and control of the hiring process. When you actually recruit, you earn it and everyone wins. Experienced Recruiters who still believe in building a real desk know exactly what I am talking about.

It is also about networking with purpose and allowing yourself thinking time to analyze the market, refine your approach, and build real strategies instead of reacting. When you operate in a true 360 full desk model, take ownership of business development, and specialize in a niche, something shifts. You start advising within a market. Recruiting is influence, intelligence, strategy, and discipline.

comment_text: There’s a subtle economic nuance embedded in the “who is the product” framing. In the traditional recruiting model, the candidate is still the product — presented, evaluated, and ultimately “purchased” by the employer. The *company* simply funds the search. Reverse recruiting doesn’t eliminate that dynamic. It shifts **who pays for representation,** not who functions as the asset being matched. Which makes this trend read much more like a talent-agent model — similar to what we see in professional sports. ✅ Recruiters resemble scouts working for **the team** (company). 🔺 Reverse recruiters resemble **agents** working for **the player** (candidate). That distinction matters because it changes expectations. ◀️ Especially at the leadership level, the meaningful success metric isn’t interview volume. It’s offer conversion.** Interviews can be generated. Offers remain market-driven decisions.
